topic.name: The Domain of a Multivariable Function

question.text: Evaluate $z = \dfrac{2y - x}{x^3 - y^2 - 4}$ at the point $(2,-2).$
question.explanation: To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,-2),$ we substitute $x = 2$ and $y = -2$ into the function expression: \begin{align*} z \, \Big|_{(2,-2)} & = \dfrac{2y - x}{x^3 - y^2 - 4} \, \Bigg|_{(2,-2)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2(-2) - 2}{2^3 - (-2)^2 - 4}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{-4 - 2}{8 - 4 - 4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-6)}{0}, \end{align*} which is undefined.

question.text: Evaluate $z = 2^{-x} + \dfrac{1}{y}$ at the point $\left(2,2\right).$
question.explanation: To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $\left(2,2\right),$ we substitute $x = 2$ and $y = 2$ into the function expression: \begin{align*} z \, \Big|_{\left(2,2\right)} & = \left(2^{-x} + \dfrac{1}{y}\right) \Bigg|_{(2,2)} \\[5pt] & = 2^{-2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2^2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{4} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Two-Variable Function

question.text: Evaluate $z = x^2+xy-5$ at the point $(1, 2).$
question.explanation:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(1, 2),$ we substitute $x=1$ and $y=2$ into the function expression:

\begin{align*} z \, \Big|_{(1,2)} &= (x^2+xy-5) \, \Big|_{(1, 2)} \\[5pt] &= (1)^2 + (1)(2) - 5 \\[5pt] &= -2 \end{align*}

question.text: The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as \[ f(x,y) = x\arccos(y+1). \] Evaluate this function at the point $(-3,1).$
question.explanation: To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(-3,1),$ we substitute $x = -3$ and $y = 1$ into the function expression: \begin{align*} f(-3,1) & = x\arccos(y+1) \, \Big|_{(-3,1)} \\[5pt] & = -3\arccos(1+1) \\[5pt] & = -3\arccos{2}, \end{align*} which is undefined.

example.title: Evaluating a Two-Variable Function

question.text: Evaluate $z = \ln(3x - 2y + 4)$ at the point $(-4,1).$
question.explanation: To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(-4,1),$ we substitute $x = -4$ and $y = 1$ into the function expression: \begin{align*} z \, \Big|_{(-4,1)} & = \ln(3x - 2y + 4) \, \Big|_{(-4,1)} \\[5pt] & = \ln(3(-4) - 2(1) + 4)\\[5pt] & = \ln(-12 - 2 + 4)\\[5pt] &= \ln(-10), \end{align*} which is undefined.

exampleAnswers.title: The Domain of a Function Involving Reciprocals and Radicals

question.text: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac {1}{2x+ y}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

\[ 2x+ y \neq 0 \]

Therefore, the domain is

\[ \big\{ (x,y) \in\mathbb R^2\,:\, 2x+ y \neq 0 \big\}. \]

Therefore, the domain is

question.text: Find the domain of the function $z = \dfrac {\sqrt {y-x^2}}{2x-y}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

\[ \begin{cases} y -x^2 \geq 0 \\[5pt] 2x-y \neq 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} y\geq x^2 \\[5pt] y \neq 2x \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the domain is

\[ \big\{ (x,y) \in\mathbb R^2\,:\, y\geq x^2, \: y \neq 2x\big\}. \]

question.text: Find the domain of the function $z = \dfrac {1}{\sqrt {1 -x^2 -y^2}}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

  • the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

\begin{align*} 1 -x^2 -y^2 \gt 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x^2 + y^2 \lt 1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the domain is \[ \big\{ (x,y) \in\mathbb R^2\,:\, x^2 + y^2 \lt 1 \big\}. \]

question.text: Find the domain of the function $z=\dfrac{x^3}{\ln (x^2-y^2)}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

\[ \begin{cases} x^2-y^2 > 0 \\[5pt] \ln(x^2-y^2) \neq 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x^2-y^2 > 0 \\[5pt] x^2-y^2 \neq 1 \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the domain is

\[ \big\{(x, y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x^2-y^2 >0, \: x^2-y^2 \neq 1 \big\}. \]

question.text: Find the domain of the function $f(x, y) = \dfrac{\ln(1 - x^2)}{y}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

\[ \begin{cases} 1-x^2 > 0 \\[5pt] y \neq 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} -1 \lt x \lt 1 \\[5pt] y \neq 0 \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the domain is

\[ \left \{(x, y) \in\mathbb R^2\, : \, -1 \lt x \lt 1, \, y \neq 0\right \}. \]

question.text: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{\ln(x-y)}{e^x}.$
question.explanation:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

  • The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

  • the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

Notice that $e^x > 0 $ for all $x.$ Therefore, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

\begin{align*} x-y > 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x > y \end{align*} Therefore, the domain is

\[ \big\{(x, y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, x > y \big\}. \]
